---
title: "Future directions"
subtitle: "Use cases, candidate components, and the shapes we might build next"
---

OpenSASE is growing into **two halves**, deliberately:

1. **The SASE half** — a policy-driven TLS-inspection edge for teams and
   servers (what the [Roadmap](roadmap.qmd) mainly tracks).
2. **The home-appliance half** — install it at home like a Pi-hole: every
   device (phone, laptop, TV) routes through it, and you get what a DNS
   blocker alone never gives you — **visibility** (what every device does),
   **control** (block/splice/bump per device and category), and
   **malware + DLP verdicts** on the traffic you choose to decrypt.

Design rule for the second half: **lightweight-first, containerized
everything.** Components must run happily on a Pi 5 / N100 mini-PC next to
the existing four containers — anything needing more gets parked (section on
GPU/ML below). Modularity is a deployment property: a compose-profile design
([#29](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/29)) will make the
**bare-minimum decrypt edge** (dnsmasq + openvpn + mitmproxy) installable on
its own, with scanner, DNS-policy, agent-inspection, and chat modules as
opt-ins.

Each numbered item below links its tracking issue. Nothing here has dates —
sequencing is by dependency, and the [board](https://github.com/users/shsingh/projects/5)
carries Area/Target per card.

## Home appliance: per-device policy + family visibility

Devices are identified by their VPN client certificate CN;
[`nix run .#vpn-getclient`](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase#client-setup)
already produces per-device profiles — policy just reads the CN. Passlist /
bumplist decisions gain an optional device dimension: kids' tablet gets
social-media blocked after 8pm, parents' laptop splices everything. A
family dashboard rides the #16 metrics/export work: verdict counts per
device, top domains, blocked events. The trust bootstrap (installing the
appliance CA on family devices, with per-device splice-only opt-out) is
treated as an honest documentation problem, not a hand-wave.

→ [#19](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/19) · depends on #8
(arm64 images — the Pi 5 *is* arm64), #15, #16

## Agent traffic: MCP as a policy category

Agents ride your VPN and call MCP servers. The protocol makes this
inspectable: the remote transport is Streamable HTTP (JSON-RPC over HTTP
POST, optional SSE), and spec drafts add request-metadata headers
(`Mcp-Method`, `Mcp-Name`) so intermediaries can inspect without parsing
payloads. So a tool call is just another HTTP category: passlist trusted
servers (splice), bump untrusted ones and scan tool arguments *and* tool
responses for prompt-injection shapes and credential leakage, logging every
`tools/call` into the decision log with the tool name.

The OpenSASE angle: MCP gateways (ContextForge, agentgateway, ToolHive,
Docker MCP Gateway — solid, containerized projects) enforce *inside their
deployment*; an agent that bypasses its gateway still rides this network.
Gateway + network-edge inspection are layers of one design, not
competitors. Patterns seeded from the inspection proxies' published
taxonomies (MCPProxy's schema quarantine, Pipelock's 48-credential /
25-injection pattern reference). Limits stated plainly: stdio transports
never touch the network; mTLS'd servers can be spliced or blocked, not read.

→ [#20](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/20) · LLM provider
egress (per-device authorization + counters, deliberately without a full AI
gateway) is [#21](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/21)

## QUIC / HTTP-3: keep decrypt-and-block honest

Browsers race to QUIC; an inspection edge that ignores UDP/443 leaks policy
(same class of leak as IPv6 bypass, #13). Two stages: **fail-closed first**
(block UDP/443, steer clients back to H2 via DNS HTTPS records —
config-only), then real interception: mitmproxy 11 already ships full
HTTP/3 support (aioquic-based), with the known caveat that Chrome distrusts
private CAs for QUIC (bump path wants a publicly trusted cert; splice is
unaffected).

→ [#22](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/22)

## Short-lived device identity (step-ca)

The architectural answer to certificate renewal: step-ca (Smallstep,
Apache-2.0, its own container) issues 24-hour device certs that renew
themselves at two-thirds lifetime. Rotation stops being an event — the
failure mode behind issue #3 largely disappears, revocation becomes
expiration, phones re-enroll silently. Mixed-mode with the existing easy-rsa
PKI documented; expiry checks become trivial.

→ [#23](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/23) · complements #11

## DNS-layer policy

Verdicts start at name resolution: dnsmasq (already in-stack) gains RPZ
zones from the same category philosophy, per-device sinkholing, and DNS
query logging joined into the decision log — device attribution begins
before TLS. Feeds reuse the signed-feed design from #14.

→ [#25](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/25)

## DLP verdicts: LEAK_BLOCK joins INFECTED

The malware verdict generalizes into a verdict family: the bump path scans
egress for secret/credential patterns; positive verdict blocks and logs
`LEAK_BLOCK` exactly like `INFECTED`. Detector rules from MIT-licensed
gitleaks rule sets (rules-as-data); feeds slot into #14's signed format.

→ [#26](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/26)

## Chat on the edge: Prosody XMPP (with stated limits)

The family chat server runs on the appliance: **Prosody** (MIT, Lua,
genuinely lightweight). An inspection component attaches via XEP-0114
(external components, verified) and XEP-0356 Privileged Entity where
moderation needs it: metadata logging, MUC moderation, spam filters for
kids' accounts — all shaped as decision-log verdicts.

The good bit: **file-transfer scanning.** Attachments sent through the chat
server's http.upload (XEP-0363) flow through the same bump + ClamAV verdict
path as any HTTPS egress — family chat attachments get INFECTED /
LEAK_BLOCK verdicts like everything else.

The hard limit, stated up front: **OMEMO (XEP-0384) end-to-end encryption
makes message content invisible to any server-side component by design**
(that is the spec's own threat model). We see metadata, unencrypted
fallback traffic, and file transfers — not OMEMO content, ever. Bumping
third-party providers' XMPP is certificate hell and is not planned.

→ [#27](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/27)

## Parked: identity-aware access (ZTNA-lite) and GPU/ML

Two directions are deliberately behind the rest:

- **ZTNA-lite** — publish internal services behind per-identity policy (the
  VPN cert *is* the identity; lean variant is a mitmproxy addon, full
  variant is Pomerium). Waits for the appliance basics to land.
  → [#24](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/24)
- **GPU/ML module** — semantic DLP, prompt-injection classifiers, a local
  LLM judge on suspicious payloads. Needs real hardware and a licensing
  conversation (the Python ML stack is Apache-2.0-heavy; in-process
  imports would conflict with our GPLv2 — everything model-shaped ships as
  its own container). → [#28](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/28)

## Last, not least: post-quantum ciphers

The deliberate last item: a PQ survey of every crypto hop (OpenVPN control
channel via TLS 1.3/OpenSSL ML-KEM hybrids, data-channel cipher reality,
mitmproxy and QUIC crypto paths) ending in a position statement and
experiment plan. No hype until the appliance roadmap lands.

→ [#30](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/30)

## Licensing ground rules (binding on all of the above)

OpenSASE's own code imports only MIT/BSD/LGPL/GPL-2-family code —
**Apache-2.0 is never imported in-process** (GPLv2-incompatible). Apache-2.0,
GPL-3, and AGPL components ship as separate containers, never vendored. The
release pipeline's SBOMs will carry per-component license fields (see the
[#7](https://github.com/shsingh/opensase/issues/7) acceptance criteria) so
this stays auditable as the component list grows. Nix satisfies GPL
source-offer structurally: every shipped binary builds from the public flake.
